content: An aura is a perceptual disturbance that some individuals experience prior to a migraine headache or an epileptic seizure. It is often characterized by the perception of unusual lights or unpleasant smells. However, the presence of an aura does not necessarily indicate that a migraine or seizure will follow, and not all individuals with migraines or epilepsy experience auras. Auras, while often unpleasant and irritating, can serve a protective function. For individuals with epilepsy, the aura provides a warning, allowing them to take precautions to prevent injury. The time between the onset of an aura and the subsequent migraine or seizure can range from a few seconds to an hour. Most individuals who experience auras report consistent types of auras each time. Classification of Auras: Auras can manifest in various forms, including: Auditory: Hearing voices or sounds that do not exist, which are true auditory hallucinations. Sensory: This includes olfactory auras, where individuals perceive strange smells, or tactile sensations such as numbness or tingling on one side of the face or body. Visual: These may include bright lights, zigzag lines, distortions in the size or shape of objects, shimmering or pulsating patches (often curved), tunnel vision, blind or dark spots in the visual field, a curtain-like effect over one eye, slowly spreading spots, kaleidoscope-like effects, or temporary monocular blindness (as seen in retinal migraines). Olfactory: Perception of strange smells, which may also be described as déjà vu or dreamlike sensations. The specific type of aura experienced may be linked to the area of the brain involved. Causes: Auras can be associated with various conditions, including: Absence seizures Color blindness Complex partial seizures Epilepsy Familial hemiplegic migraine Focal seizures Gluten-sensitive enteropathy-associated conditions Migraines Partial seizures Physiologic nonepileptic seizures Pituitary adenoma Simple partial seizures Temporal lobe epilepsy Tonic-clonic seizures History and Symptoms: When evaluating a patient with auras, it is important to consider: The type of aura experienced Family history of similar conditions Activities associated with the onset of the aura Known triggers Symptoms following the aura, such as loss of consciousness or difficulty speaking (aphasia) Any prior trauma Physical Examination: A thorough physical examination should include: A complete head and neck examination A comprehensive neurologic examination Laboratory Findings: Laboratory tests may include: Complete blood count (CBC) Calcium, magnesium, and glucose levels Blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and creatinine levels Imaging and Diagnostic Studies: CT scans: Useful for evaluating trauma or physiologic seizures. MRI: Helps rule out cerebral pathology. Electroencephalogram (EEG): Used to detect seizure activity. Toxicology screen: May be performed to rule out toxic causes. Treatment: Management of auras involves: Avoidance of known triggers (especially for migraines) Stabilization of patients experiencing status epilepticus Pharmacotherapy: Acute pharmacologic treatments include: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) for migraines 5-HT1 agonists for migraines Acetaminophen for migraines Intravenous benzodiazepines for epilepsy Antiepileptic drugs for epilepsy Additional Symptoms of Auras: Feelings of detachment from one’s body Sensations of limbs moving independently from the body Anxiety or fear Nausea Weakness or unsteadiness Difficulty understanding or comprehending spoken words during or after the aura Inability to speak properly despite understanding what one wants to say (aphasia) Feelings of power or euphoria, which may occur in some individuals discontinuing seizure treatments The specific sensations associated with an aura can sometimes help localize the focus of a seizure. It is important to note that while auras share some symptoms with strokes, the onset of an aura is typically more gradual.
